edges.mechanism: High debt-to-GDP ratio (122%) signals potential government insolvency risk
Projected net interest outlays of 3.6% of GDP raise concerns about fiscal capacity
Sustainability concerns impose binding constraints on central bank autonomy
Debt sustainability fears increase market perception of potential central bank monetization
Market participants price fiscal dominance risk into long-duration Treasury premiums
Widening deficits sustain elevated real long-term rates through crowding-out pressure
High real rates make capital projects unprofitable at historical return thresholds
Elevated public debt reduces effectiveness of future fiscal stimulus
High debt triggers household expectations of future tax liabilities
Anticipation of future taxes leads households to increase savings
Increased savings partially offsets expansionary fiscal impulses, suppressing demand
Reduced multiplier diminishes fiscal stimulus impact on aggregate demand, confounded by Ricardian effects

summary: The passage describes a fiscal-monetary feedback loop in which elevated debt-to-GDP ratios and rising net interest outlays raise sovereign debt sustainability concerns. These concerns constrain monetary policy independence and elevate fiscal dominance risk, which markets price into higher Treasury term premiums. Widening fiscal deficits crowd out private investment by sustaining high real long-term interest rates. Simultaneously, elevated public debt reduces the fiscal multiplier through Ricardian equivalence: households anticipate future tax liabilities, increase precautionary savings, and thereby partially offset expansionary fiscal impulses, ultimately suppressing aggregate demand growth.
